newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Deane spurns job offers to stay at beloved Telecom.
newsitem.headline: Deane spurns job offers to stay at beloved Telecom.

text.p: Telecom chief executive Roderick Deane loves his job and has rejected other lucrative offers in order to remain at the helm of New Zealand's largest listed company.
In an interview with Reuters, Deane spoke enthusiastically of his demanding role and indicated he would not willingly move, even to become the Governor of the Reserve Bank.
"I love the (telecommunications) industry -- it is such a fascinating, stimulating industry," he said.
"I've got no present intentions of moving anywhere."
Since taking the reins in November 1992, Deane guided Telecom through a tumultuous period after the telephone utility was controversially privatised in 1990.

A consumate businessman with a doctorate in economics, Deane presided over a reform process which radically cut Telecom's staff from around 26,000 to under 9,000 today, and set the company on the path to increasingly large profits.
Telecom is expected to make a record profit of over NZ$800 million in the 1997/98 financial year.
But the rigours of the rapidly evolving telecommunications industry are not conducive to management longevity either.
Deane's main foe on the business battlefield, Clear Communications chief executive Andrew Makin, earlier this month surprise the industry by resigning.
Makin said he was leaving for a lifestyle change.
Deane was critical of the litigious approach of Clear, which is quarter owned each by British Telecom and its U.S. partner MCI Communications Corp.
"We were always sorry that they (Clear) felt the need to blame other people, whether it be government or Telecom or anyone else in the industry, over and over again for their problems.
"But in terms of why Mr Makim has decided to go when the industry is so exciting and challenging and fun, and he's not yet really at retirement age, I don't know," Deane said.

The success of Deane's management style and business strategies, achieved in an increasingly competitive marketplace, has led to speculation he was being headhunted by other corporates, among them Fletcher Challenge Ltd where he is already a director.
Deane declined to comment on specific job offers, but said he was happy where he was.
"Put it this way: have I had other job offers? Yes. Am I going to accept them? No."

Deane was chief executive at Electricity Corp of New Zealand for five years before moving to Telecom. He has a string of high-ranking posts to his credit, including Deputy Reserve Bank Governor from 1982 to 1986.
Indeed, he has been touted as a possible successor to present central bank governor Don Brash.
Deane rejected the suggestion, almost.
"Don Brash is doing a fantastic job. Why would I want to replace somebody who is doing such a splendid job? I think he's brilliant at that job," he said.
Moreover, I don't think anybody would offer it to me."
--Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
